meta.title: Landscaping in Swartz Creek, MI | Grand Scapes
meta.description: Grand Scapes rebuilds tired beds in Swartz Creek, MI: overgrown 1950s and 60s shrubs dug out, new block or natural borders, and beds planned for wet ground.

hero.title: Old shrubs, **out by the roots.**
hero.lede: Grand Scapes rebuilds Swartz Creek front yards: overgrown foundation shrubs and small trees dug out with a track loader, beds reshaped with a block wall or a clean natural edge, then new plants and mulch.

local.title: Older homes, wet soil and **small fronts.**
local.intro: Most of Swartz Creek's single family homes went up in the 1950s and 60s, and many of their front beds show it: shrubs grown into the windows, old brick borders sunk into the dirt, beds that have shrunk or sprawled over the years. Underneath, the city's plan notes a high water table and wet, slow draining soil. A good bed here has to account for both.

points.title: Shrubs grown into the windows
points.body: A shrub planted decades ago has usually outgrown its spot. We dig them out with a compact track loader, roots and all, and the bed starts over. One of our reviews describes 25 year old bushes and a cherry tree coming out and a new bed going in. More on [bush removal](/bush-removal/).

points.title: Beds placed around wet spots
points.body: Where water sits after rain decides where a bed goes and what goes in it. Rob looks at the low spots before he suggests a shape, and plants that need dry roots stay out of them.

points.title: Small fronts near the sidewalk
points.body: Lots in neighborhoods like Park, Elms and Atkins Acres are mostly small, according to the city's plan, and the front bed sits a few steps from the public walk. A crisp border and plants that stay in scale make the whole front look kept.

points.title: Brick edging swapped for block
points.body: Old brick edging can sink and let mulch spill into the lawn. A gray block wall or a cut natural edge replaces it, keeps the mulch in and gives the mower a clean line to follow.

logistics.title: How a Swartz Creek bed makeover runs.
body: Rob comes out first, looks at the beds, the light, the drainage and what is worth keeping, and tells you plainly what he would do. You get a price, then a date.

On a city lot the track loader and dump trailer come in from the street, so the crew plans where they sit and keeps the public sidewalk open and swept. Old shrubs, roots and soil go in the trailer and leave with us, because the city's curbside yard waste and brush chipping are sized for bundled trimmings and branches no thicker than 4 inches.

We do not take down big trees. For a yard that needs regrading or new seed after the old beds come out, ask about [grading and new lawns](/grading-and-new-lawns/), and finish the beds with fresh [mulch](/mulch-installation-swartz-creek-mi/).

facts.label: Borders
facts.value: Gray block wall or a natural edge

faq.q: Do you do landscaping in Swartz Creek, MI?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes does landscaping in Swartz Creek: tearing out overgrown beds, digging out bushes and small trees, new borders in gray block or a cut natural edge, and new plants and mulch. The estimate is free, and Rob suggests what the yard needs.

faq.q: Can you remove old bushes from the front of my house?
faq.a: Yes. We dig overgrown bushes and small trees out with a compact track loader, roots included, so the bed can be rebuilt, and the debris goes in our trailer. Big trees are a job for a tree company, and Rob will say so if that is what you have.

faq.q: What can be done about a bed that stays wet?
faq.a: It depends on why it is wet. Much of Swartz Creek sits along the creek's floodplain, and the city's plan describes a high water table and poor drainage. Sometimes the answer is a new shape or grade so water moves away from the house; sometimes it is picking plants that handle wet ground. Rob would rather see it after a rain.

faq.q: Do you replace old brick edging?
faq.a: Yes. Old brick borders come out and get replaced with a gray block wall or a cut natural edge, whichever suits the bed and the house. A good edge keeps mulch where it belongs and gives the lawn a clean line.
